story: The Hallingskarvet massif rests on the plateaus around it, with steep scarps to north and south and Folarskardnuten, 1,933 metres, on its top. Between the barren summit plateau and the greener land below runs the sheer edge that gave the mountain its name: skarv means bare mountain. The rock of the plateau is Precambrian plutonic rock, part of the Caledonian mountain chain, thrust up and over softer sedimentary layers. Erosion has stripped away the land around it, leaving the hard gneiss standing proud above the plateaus, and deep cirques bite into the plateau from the north.

Several ice ages shaped the landscape, and the park was created partly to keep a landform that explains the geological history of Norway. It takes in the Hallingskarv plateau and the high mountains to its west, the Vargebreen glacier and the valleys of Såtedalen, Lengjedalen, Ynglesdalen and part of Raggsteindalen. Flakavatnet lies in a hollow of the massif at 1,453 metres.

Life on the mountain is hard, but some have learned to cope. Wild reindeer roam the area all year in search of grazing — once part of the same herd as Hardangervidda's, now largely separated from it by the Bergen Line. Lime- and phyllite-rich ground feeds a surprisingly lush flora: the glacier buttercup turns to follow the sun, purple saxifrage flowers within days of the snow leaving, and threatened species such as the lance-leaf grapefern grow here. Arctic foxes live in the park, and golden eagles, gyrfalcons, kestrels and rough-legged buzzards hunt over it.

People have trapped reindeer here since prehistory. From the 1600s to the 1800s drovers took horses and cattle over the mountain to trade each summer, and the simple overnight shelters they used can still be seen. In 1880 the English Lord Garvagh, who came to hunt reindeer, built a dry-stone hut in Folarskardet, and the philosopher Arne Næss wrote about the mountain from his cabin, Tvergastein. The park was created on 22 December 2006.
howItWorks: The right to roam, allemannsretten, applies: you may walk anywhere in the outfield, camp for two nights in one place without asking — longer high in the mountains — at least 150 metres from a house or cabin, and pick berries and mushrooms. Careful use of wood for campfires is allowed, though there is little of it above the tree line. From 15 April to 15 September it is forbidden across Norway to light a fire in or near forest and other open country unless the municipality has allowed it or a fire plainly cannot spread; check with Hol, Ulvik or Aurland before you go. Dogs must be on a lead from 1 April to 20 August under the national dog law.

Motor traffic is forbidden on land, on water and in the air below 300 metres; e-bikes count, and drones may not be flown. Under Miljødirektoratet's rule, drones may not take off in a national park or be flown into one without the park board's permission, and motor-driven model aircraft are banned. Cycling and organised riding are allowed only on routes or in areas approved in the management plan. Motor traffic on snow for the Skarverennet ski race is a fixed exception, and preparing ski trails by machine needs a permit.

Organised walking is fine as long as it does no harm; organised activities that could damage the environment need permission. Hunting, trapping and fishing follow the ordinary laws. Give the wild reindeer a wide berth: they are easily disturbed and the mountain is their year-round range.

sightNotes.poi-no-hallingskarvet-folarskardnuten: The highest point of Hallingskarvet, 1,933 metres, on the summit plateau above the north and south scarps.
sightNotes.poi-no-hallingskarvet-prestholtskarvet: The eastern end of the massif. A 6.5 km path from Prestholtseter, partly paved in stone by Sherpas from Nepal, climbs to a viewpoint at 1,705 metres.
sightNotes.poi-no-hallingskarvet-folarskardet: A pass through the massif, where Lordehytta, the dry-stone hut of the reindeer-hunting Lord Garvagh, has stood since 1880.
sightNotes.poi-no-hallingskarvet-flakavatnet: A high, cold lake at 1,453 metres in a hollow of the massif's western end.
sightNotes.poi-no-hallingskarvet-vargebreen: Also written Vargabreen: the glacier in the high mountains at the park's western end.
sightNotes.poi-no-hallingskarvet-raggsteindalen: A valley on the north side of the massif, partly inside the park.

entrances: Finse, Haugastøl and Ustaoset stations on the Bergen Line, along the southern boundary
Geilo, the national park village at the foot of the mountain

planYourVisit.reservations: No booking or fee. Marked routes run around the plateau in summer and winter, and the trekking association's Finsehytta and Geiterygghytta stand on the south and north sides of the western end.

Drones and any motor use need a permit
camping: Wild camping under the right to roam

chronology.text: Repeated glaciations carve the cirques and strip the land around the hard gneiss of the massif.
Hunters build trapping systems for wild reindeer on the mountain.
Drovers cross the mountain each summer with horses and cattle for trade, sheltering in simple overnight camps.
Lord Garvagh, an English reindeer hunter, builds the dry-stone Lordehytta in Folarskardet.
The Bergen Line opens along the foot of the mountain, later separating Hallingskarvet's reindeer from Hardangervidda's.
Hallingskarvet National Park is created on 22 December.

safety: The scarps are hundreds of metres high and the summit plateau is flat and featureless in fog. Keep well back from the edges and navigate carefully in poor visibility.
Weather on the plateau is far harsher than at the stations below; carry warm, windproof clothing even in summer.
In snow, keep well back from the rim of the scarps, which may be corniced.
regulations: No motor traffic on land, water or in the air below 300 metres; no e-bikes or drones without a permit.
Cycling and organised riding only on approved routes.
No open fires in or near forest from 15 April to 15 September unless the municipality allows it.
Dogs on a lead from 1 April to 20 August.

weather: This is high mountain country, and on the summit plateau the climate is harsher and the soil poorer than on the slopes below. Summer brings marked walking routes, flowering slopes and fishing in the lakes around the plateau; in late winter and spring the marked ski routes come into their own, and the Skarverennet race runs from Finse to Ustaoset through the park.
directions: Hallingskarvet lies in the heart of southern Norway, about four hours by train or car from both Oslo and Bergen. The Bergen Line runs along the southern boundary, with stations at Geilo, Ustaoset, Haugastøl and Finse; no public road reaches Finse, so at the park's western end the train is one of the few ways in. Rv 7 runs to the south, and Fv 50 follows Strandavatnet on the north side. The Rallarvegen passes just outside the park.
